notes.meaning: Paul tells the Corinthians that he is getting ready to visit them for the third time. He quotes the Old Testament rule that any serious charge must be confirmed by two or three witnesses. This means he will not act on mere rumors, but will carry out a fair and careful inquiry when he arrives.

Paul repeats the warning he gave during his earlier visit. He warns those who fell into sin before, as well as anyone else disobeying God, that he will take firm action if they do not repent. When he comes in person, he will not hold back the church discipline they need.

Some in Corinth had demanded proof that Christ was really speaking through Paul. Paul reminds them that Christ is never weak toward them, but has already shown His power in their church. If they keep testing Christ's authority in Paul, they will feel that power through sharp discipline.

Jesus appeared weak when He was crucified and surrendered His life, but He now lives by the mighty power of God. In the same way, Paul shares in Christ's humble appearance and earthly weakness. Yet by God's power, he lives with Christ and will act with spiritual strength to guide and correct the church.

Paul tells the believers to look closely at their own lives instead of sitting in judgment on him. They need to test themselves to see whether they are truly living in the faith and whether Christ lives within them. Unless they fail that test, their own spiritual life proves that Paul's preaching was true.

differ.view: This test is about whether a person has truly been converted and saved, urging churchgoers to make sure their faith is genuine.
Paul assumed the Corinthians were already Christians and was urging them to check whether their daily conduct matched the faith they professed.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Believers can know that they hold the Christian faith, but they cannot have absolute certainty that they are in a state of grace or will be saved.

notes.meaning: Paul is confident the believers will realize that he and his fellow workers have not failed the test. Their work in Corinth was real, and God had clearly approved their ministry. If the Corinthians recognize Christ in themselves, they must also accept the teacher through whom they believed.

Paul prays earnestly that the Corinthians will do what is right and turn away from all wrongdoing. His main desire is not to prove his apostolic power by having to punish people. He would much rather look weak and unproven, so long as they walk in holiness.

Paul explains that church leaders have no power to work against God's truth. Their authority from the Lord can only be used to defend and promote what is right. As long as the believers walk in the truth of the gospel, Paul has no reason to discipline them.

Paul is glad to seem weak whenever the Corinthians are spiritually strong and need no rebuke. His deepest prayer is for their complete restoration. He uses a picture like setting broken bones back into place, wanting their divisions healed and every member standing united.

Paul writes these strong warnings ahead of time so he will not need to be severe when he arrives. The Lord gave him authority to build up the church, not to tear people down. He hopes his letter leads them to repent now so his upcoming visit can be peaceful.

Paul closes his letter with warm words of encouragement, telling the church members to rejoice and pursue spiritual wholeness. He urges them to comfort one another, agree in love, and live in peace. When believers live together in harmony, the God of love and peace promises to dwell with them.

Paul tells the believers to greet one another with a holy kiss. In their culture, this was a pure and customary sign of family affection and mutual forgiveness. It showed that old quarrels were forgotten and that the church stood together as one body.

Paul sends greetings from all the believers in the place where he was writing, likely Macedonia. In the early church, all Christians were called saints, which means people set apart for God. This simple greeting reminded the Corinthians that they belonged to a larger family of believers.

Paul ends with a famous closing prayer that names all three persons of the Trinity: the Son, the Father, and the Holy Spirit. He asks for Jesus Christ's undeserved kindness, God the Father's deep love, and the Holy Spirit's shared life and fellowship to rest on all of them. This blessing shows that true peace comes from sharing in the life of God.
